description: We are a young and ambitious team of students who strive to achieve serenity through space-related activities. Our signal-to-noise ratio is low, but our enthusiasm has infinite gain. We believe in teamwork, open data, and the healing power of a well-calibrated antenna. Mission status: nominal, mostly caffeinated, and accelerating.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator tells mission planners where and when a lander at the lunar south pole will have sunlight for power and a direct line to Earth. At the pole the Sun and Earth move a few degrees above the horizon, so a single mountain decides the answer: on a smooth-sphere model the Haworth crater floor sees the Sun half the time, with real terrain never.
We traced the horizon from every point of a 480 × 480 km polar region in 360 directions over NASA LOLA elevation models, then tracked the Sun and Earth with JPL's DE440 ephemeris every 10 minutes for a year (Nov 2026 – Nov 2027). Two zones at 500 m resolution cover the pole and Mons Mouton.
The browser workbench works like a chip-design tool. Planners set mission constraints: landing-zone slope and relief, sunlit days, Earth contact, solar energy, longest night. Each becomes a map layer, their intersection shows where landing works, and a search lists the earliest feasible dates and places. Examples apply the requirements of Apollo 17, IM-2 and Blue Ghost 1. LRO and Danuri relay passes, DSN coverage, a horizon panorama and CSV/JSON export complete it.
Results match NASA's independent polar illumination maps (r = 0.994). The app runs offline in any browser.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator

The problem
Artemis III and the next robotic landers are going to the lunar south pole. It has water ice in craters that never see the Sun, and ridges that are lit almost all the time. Every mission there asks two questions: will the lander have sunlight for power, and a direct line to Earth for communication? At the pole both the Sun and the Earth move only a few degrees above the horizon, so the answer depends on the mountains around the lander, not on latitude. A model of the Moon as a smooth sphere gets it wrong in both directions. Over one year, the floor of Haworth crater would see the Sun 50% of the time on a sphere, and 0% with the real terrain. The ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache would see it 52% of the time on a sphere, and 79% with the real terrain.

What we built
An engineering workbench for choosing a landing site and date. It is laid out like a chip-design tool: a map with switchable layers, an inspector, and design rules that a landing must pass.
- Mission constraints: landing-zone size, maximum slope and height difference, Sun and Earth at touchdown, minimum sunlit days, minimum days in contact with Earth, minimum solar energy in kWh per m² of panel, longest night, longest loss of contact. Each constraint is its own map layer, and one more layer shows where all of them hold at once.
- Nearest landings: the tool checks every place and every 6-hour landing slot in the year and lists the earliest dates and places that meet every requirement.
- Examples from flown missions: the requirements of Apollo 17, IM-2 Athena and Blue Ghost Mission 1, applied in one click.
- Exact values for any point: Sun and Earth elevation and azimuth, the terrain horizon in that direction, and the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earthrise, to 10 minutes.
- Communication: passes of the LRO and Danuri relay orbiters and the Deep Space Network ground stations in view.
- A 480 x 480 km overview with 3 km cells, and two 500 m detail zones (the pole and Mons Mouton) that open in place when you zoom in.
- A 360-degree panorama from the surface, a Sun-Earth-Moon view, and CSV/JSON export.

How it works
From every cell we traced the horizon 150 km in 360 directions over NASA LOLA elevation models, taking the Moon's curvature into account. JPL DE440 ephemeris gives the Sun and the Earth every 10 minutes for a year, from November 2026 to November 2027. Visibility is computed for 25,600 places per region at 52,560 moments, and searches across the whole region run in the browser in under a second.

Proof it is right
- Our Sun visibility matches NASA Goddard's independent polar illumination maps cell by cell, with a correlation of 0.994 and an average difference of about 1 percentage point.
- The Sun's position matches JPL Horizons to within 0.05 degrees.
- With strict requirements, the search finds the Malapert massif and the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge without being told where to look. NASA has named both as Artemis III candidate regions.
- The IM-2 Athena requirements hold at IM-2's real landing site.
- The tool also shows why resolution matters. At 3 km resolution the IM-2 site seems to get 6% Sun. At 500 m it gets 42%, against NASA's 45%.

Why it matters
A planner enters the mission's needs once and sees on a single map where and when they can be met, with every rule shown separately. When the launch date slips, they move the timeline instead of starting a new study. The app runs offline in any browser, with no installation.
